title: I Used AI to Do Product Discovery on My Own Idea
text: Medium I Used AI to Do Product Discovery on My Own Idea | by Aditya Nanda Tri Prakoso | Sep, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Medium Logo Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in The first idea didn’t survive discovery Finding the problem underneath the problem Then I challenged the new idea too Turning my opinions into assumptions Discovery became increasingly about trust The prototype became another discovery tool What I actually learned from doing discovery with AI Artificial Intelligence Product Management Product Discovery Gym Workout Prototyping I Used AI to Do Product Discovery on My Own Idea Aditya Nanda Tri Prakoso 9 min read · Sep 24, 2026 -- Listen Share I use Hevy for almost every workout. It tracks my exercises, sets, reps, weights and history, which means something slightly funny happens every time I train: the app knows what I did, but I still have to decide what I should do next. Should I increase the weight? Should I stay where I am? Was that set hard because the weight was too high, or because I’m just fatigued today? Should I push for a PR, or repeat what worked last time? None of these decisions are particularly difficult. The problem is that they happen while I’m supposed to be training. I want to focus on the exercise, not spend the session thinking about programming. That was the starting point for this project. I had a small annoyance with Hevy: I increasingly use generative AI to create or adjust workout programmes, but once I have the plan, I still have to manually recreate it inside Hevy. My first thought was therefore very straightforward: why can’t I just paste a workout plan into Hevy and have it automatically become a routine? Rather than immediately building it, I started brainstorming it with AI. Not in the sense of asking AI to invent a startup idea for me, but more like having a product thinking partner that I could continuously challenge, disagree with and ask to look at the problem from another angle. That ended up becoming the interesting part of the project: using AI throughout the entire process, from the first vague problem to the eventual prototype. The first idea didn’t survive discovery I started with a Five Whys. Why do I have to re-enter the workout? Because Hevy doesn’t automatically turn unstructured text into a routine. Why does that matter? Because the workout information already exists somewhere else. Why is that a problem? Because it creates friction between planning and execution. Why are those separate workflows? Because the planning layer and the tracking layer are disconnected. And why does that separation actually matter? That last question changed the direction of the project. My actual training loop isn’t simply Plan → Configure → Workout. It’s Plan → Execute → Track → Understand → Adapt → Plan again . Once I looked at that bigger loop, the importer started to look less interesting. I don’t create a completely new programme that often, and Hevy already provides duplication workarounds. The importer would save me some manual work, but not enough for it to feel like an important problem. Through the payment lens I was using for the exercise, it wasn’t something I was particularly convinced I would pay to solve either. So I dropped the idea. That was probably the first important discovery: the output of product discovery doesn’t have to be validation. It can be killing your own idea. Finding the problem underneath the problem With the importer gone, I started looking at what was actually happening once a workout was already inside Hevy. I had the data. What I didn’t have was interpretation. I could look at previous weights, reps, RPE and progression, but I was still the person doing the mental work of deciding whether I should push, hold, back off or change something. That led to a different problem statement: I have workout data, but I still have to do the thinking. The more I explored it with AI, the more specific the problem became. Maybe the real friction wasn’t Track → Understand, where I analyse my data after the fact. Maybe it was Understand → Decide, where I have to turn all that information into an action while I’m in the middle of a workout. That distinction mattered. I wasn’t really asking for more information. I wanted direction . The eventual need became: I don’t want to think about programming while I’m working out. I want to focus on the exercise and trust something to handle the progression decisions. The product thesis became: let the AI think about progression so I can think about training. Then I challenged the new idea too The next question was uncomfortable: why build this at all? AI could already analyse workout data. I could export my history, put it into Claude and ask it to compare sessions, identify progression or regressions and suggest what I should do next. I could even create a Claude Project and use a spreadsheet as persistent history. In other words, I could approximate a basic version of this workflow today with something like Hevy → spreadsheet → Claude → analysis → recommendation → Hevy . So simply saying “this is an AI workout analyser” wasn’t enough. That pushed me toward the workflow itself. I didn’t want to open a chatbot during my workout, provide context, wait for an answer and then translate that answer back into what I was doing. I wanted to log my sets normally and have the system already understand what was happening. That changed the concept from an AI chatbot into an AI-native training decision layer sitting on top of the tracker. Instead of giving me another place to inspect my data, it would participate in the existing workflow: observe what I had done, interpret the context and tell me whether to push, hold or back off while I kept the final decision. Turning my opinions into assumptions At this point, I had a product idea I actually liked, which created another risk: I could very easily start using AI to make my own opinions sound more rigorous.
